passage: Anand said yes to everything that carried the director's name: the launch deck, the town-hall demo, the client dashboard, the hackathon team. In his Mumbai office his calendar looked like a bus timetable. By week six he had missed the deadline on the dashboard, and then the next one, on a quarterly report. Samir, across from him at lunch, said gently, "You're on eleven things." Anand shrugged. "Visibility matters." At the review, his manager laid the list on the table: eleven activities, two late, none finished with real depth. "It looks scattered," the manager said. Anand went home wondering whether being seen and being trusted with a big goal were really the same thing.

qa.q: How many things was Anand working on?
qa.a: Anand was working on eleven things.

qa.q: How did Anand feel when Samir mentioned the eleven things?
qa.a: Anand felt defensive, shrugging it off by saying visibility matters, before the review left him unsettled.

qa.q: What could Anand do instead of taking every high-profile task, and why?
qa.a: Anand could choose two or three tasks that matter most and finish them well, because a few clear results make a stronger record than many half-done ones.

qa.q: How might Samir have felt watching Anand's schedule fill up?
qa.a: Samir was probably concerned for Anand, which is why Samir raised it gently over lunch.

grounding: Illustrates taking on every high-profile task, spreading thin and missing deadlines, so the many activities look scattered rather than strong.

passage:
"Ujjwal, you look like you haven't slept."
"I haven't, Sahil. I'm on the investor deck, the CEO's town-hall slides and the new partnership pitch."
"Aren't you also leading the pricing analysis?"
"That too. That's the promotion work. The rest is visibility. If the leadership sees my name everywhere, they'll remember me."
"And the pricing analysis is due when?"
"It was due Monday." He rubbed his eyes. "And the market report was due last Friday. I asked for more time on both."
"Two missed deadlines in one month?"
"They'll understand. Look at everything else I'm doing."
Sahil hesitated. "Our director asked me yesterday what your main project is. I didn't know what to say. It sounded like you're doing ten things halfway."
Ujjwal stopped typing.
"Maybe pick the one thing you want to be known for," Sahil said gently.

qa.q: Which two deadlines did Ujjwal miss?
qa.a: The pricing analysis, due Monday, and the market report, due last Friday.

qa.q: Why did Ujjwal stop typing when Sahil mentioned the director?
qa.a: He was likely shaken and uneasy, realising that his many visible tasks were making his record look scattered rather than strong.

qa.q: Which approach would suit Ujjwal better than chasing every high-profile task?
qa.a: He could ask his manager what the promotion really requires and focus on one or two projects that meet it, delivering them on time.

qa.q: How does Ujjwal's overload look to Sahil?
qa.a: Sahil worries about him and feels awkward, because the director asked what Ujjwal's main project is and Sahil had no clear answer.

grounding: It shows someone chasing every high-profile task, missing two deadlines and ending up with a record that looks scattered rather than strong.

passage:
Looking back, last year I tried to be everywhere.
Charu, my manager, mentioned that senior roles need visibility. I heard it as "do everything leadership can see." So I joined the culture committee, volunteered for the CEO's offsite logistics, took the hackathon, and offered to help with the new client pitch. All on top of my actual job, the claims-processing redesign.
By October I was answering emails at 1 a.m. I missed the redesign pilot date. Then I sent the pitch numbers two days late, and Charu had to present with half a slide.
In my review she was kind but clear. "Jagdish, your list is long, but I can't point to one thing you owned from start to finish. It looks scattered."
I felt my face heat up. She was right.
This year, one project, the redesign, done properly.

qa.q: What was Jagdish's actual job last year?
How did Jagdish feel when Charu called the record scattered?
qa.a: Jagdish felt embarrassed, face heating up, and also recognised with some regret that she was right.

qa.q: What else could Jagdish have done after hearing that senior roles need visibility?
qa.a: Jagdish could have asked Charu what visibility meant in practice and which one project would show it, instead of guessing and saying yes to everything.

qa.q: How was Charu affected by Jagdish taking on too much?
qa.a: Charu had to present the client pitch with half a slide because the numbers came two days late, and then had to give a hard review.

grounding: It shows someone chasing every high-profile task, missing two deadlines and ending with a record that looks scattered rather than strong.
